name: Lateral platysmapexy

card.summary: A neck-lift surgical technique that supports the platysma muscle from the sides to sharpen the jawline-to-neck contour.
card.note: Surgery performed by qualified surgeons; risks include hematoma, nerve injury and contour irregularity.

quick.overview:
Lateral platysmapexy is a neck-lift step in which a surgeon anchors the platysma, the thin neck muscle sheet, at its outer edge instead of, or alongside, stitching its middle edges together. The aim is a tighter, cleaner neck and jaw contour.

Surgical descriptions note that sources differ on the exact anchor point, and one article cited on Wikipedia states that medial plication was generally more effective than simple lateral pulling, especially for midline problems.
quick.how: It is performed by a plastic or facial plastic surgeon, usually within a facelift or neck lift, and is often combined with medial platysmaplasty, fat removal or deeper work. Recovery and downtime are set by the surgeon.
quick.risks: Reported risks of neck-lift surgery include bleeding or hematoma, infection, numbness, temporary motor nerve weakness, contour problems such as cobra neck, and recurrent bands.

lead: Lateral platysmapexy, also called lateral platysma suspension, is a type of platysmaplasty in which the platysma is supported from the side rather than repaired at the midline. It is used within neck lifts to improve neck and jawline definition.[2]

Anatomically, the platysma is a thin muscle covering the front of the neck from the upper chest to the lower jaw and mouth corner; with age it loses tone and vertical bands can appear.[3] Surgical techniques range from medial plication (corset), lateral suspension, combined approaches and vertical suspension.[2]
Researchers have described related submental techniques, such as the digastric corset, which was reported in a 20-patient series.[1]

chain: Loose neck tissue is supported and tightened
angle.text: Lateral suspension lifts and supports the neck's muscle layer, which is intended to define the jaw-neck transition. It is selected by surgeons based on the patient's anatomy.

paras: In lateral platysmapexy the muscle's free edge is fixed to tissue at the side of the neck. Sources differ on the anchor: one describes the upper sternocleidomastoid fascia, another tissue near the earlobe.[2]

Medial platysmaplasty brings the muscle edges together under the chin, while combined techniques address both parts. One study cited in the overview reported that medial work was generally more effective than lateral pulling alone for midline deformity.[2]

Neck-lift risks include hematoma, infection, numbness, temporary weakness of motor nerves, contour irregularities such as cobra neck, recurrent bands, and, when glands are treated, saliva collection or lip weakness.[2]
No studies found specific to lateral platysmapexy under this name. Related work includes a 2013 anatomical and clinical study of the digastric corset in 20 cases for submental rejuvenation.[1]
